newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed raises spectre of civil war in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Lebed raises spectre of civil war in Russia.

text.p: Charismatic general Alexander Lebed urged the Russian government to step down on Friday, saying a planned nationwide protest action later this month could lead to Albanian-style anarchy.

"On March 27 there might be a decisive stage in the crisis of the powers-that-be in all its branches at once with a move to chaos and anarchy in the country," Lebed told supporters at the opening of the first congress of his new party.

The Federation of Independent Trade Unions -- the biggest union grouping in Russia -- is threatening to stage a one-day national strike to protest against wage arrears and the government's social policies.

"Little is needed for a few provocateurs to be introduced into any crowd during peaceful protest actions on March 27 -- broken shop windows, arson attacks, looted kiosks," said Lebed, who hopes his new party will propel him into the Kremlin.

"One victim and that's it. The authorities have their hands free to introduce a state of emergency... and it is already the first step towards a suicidal civil war. We of course would win it but we don't need that kind of war, even for free," he said.
"Let little Albania become an example to us, to huge Russia. The president ran off in some unknown direction, the army declares its neutrality. It would not declare neutrality here."

Many Russians, like Albanians, have lost out in reforms which they see as benefiting a corrupt few. A wave of strikes has brought little change for the better, but talk of an armed uprising is restricted to a few isolated extremists.

Lebed, who ended Moscow's bloody 21-month conflict with Chechnya before being fired from the Kremlin by President Boris Yeltsin for overt presidential ambitions, has ridden a wave of popularity in recent months as Yeltsin suffered ill health.

While he is consistently favoured in opinion polls, he has little power base. He said his party had 10,000 members, compared with the hundreds of thousands claimed by the main opposition Communist Party.

With Yeltsin on the mend, Lebed resorted to complaining that his former boss had tried to steal his thunder in a state-of-the nation address last week in which the president called for order and promised a new, more effective government.
Lebed said his Russian Popular Republican Party stood against the use of force, but appeared to be referring to force used by the authorities.

"Tomorrow it will be published that Lebed called for an overthrow of power and incited an uprising. Be careful with such words," said the general, his face set in a frown throughout his hour-long speech.

"I rebel today against the authorities' irresponsibility and unsystematic rule, against actions aimed at destroying the state in which I have the honour to live...It is my sacred duty (to rebel) and I will not have any prosecutor tell me what to do."

The retired general said that far from showing that Yeltsin was back at the helm, his reinstatement last week of his reformist chief aide Anatoly Chubais to the cabinet was a further sign that he was being manipulated by his entourage.

"The appointment of Chubais to a key position in the government is a further...clumsy and confrontational step by the president after which you understand the full meaning of the expression 'the entourage is playing the king'".

After the speech, Lebed won a vote of approval from chess grandmaster Gary Kasparov, who said he was convinced that only Lebed could introduce order and ensure the necessary conditions for Russia's rapid economic development.
